absent: Implementation of fault, synchronization, translation and completion callbacks beyond their signatures and parameter roles.
Full tail of virtual-machine-wide x86 state beyond the truncation point and the definitions of its remaining statistics and cache-sizing companions.
Concrete semantics of CPU role, page format, root info, reverse-map heads and allocation caches referenced but not defined in these fragments.
Lock acquisition order and sleep versus atomic context for the listed mutexes, spinlocks, semaphores and sequence counters beyond the nesting notes shown.
Runtime transition rules for queued exceptions, interrupts, nonmaskable and system-management inputs beyond flag presence.
Exact bit positions and reserved-mask values for control, status, capability and filter registers beyond the enumerated modes and counts.
Behavior of hypercall, event-channel, poll-timer, recovery-thread and precise-event collection paths that use the cached pages and tables.

findings.text: Guest address translation is factored into a small descriptor that bundles four operations with execution context. The operations cover fetching the top guest paging base, reading a legacy protected-mode pointer by index, delivering a fault into the guest with a hardware-origin flag, and converting a guest virtual or physical address under an access mask with exception reporting. The descriptor also carries a CPU role view and a page-format description that parameterize those conversions.

Callers extend paging and input output handling by supplying callbacks rather than editing core flows. The page-table layer offers fault handling and single-entry synchronization hooks plus the four translation helpers named in the walk descriptor. The virtual CPU layer offers a userspace completion hook invoked after emulation defers to userspace. Each hook receives the current virtual CPU and a request-specific record, allowing vendor or mode code to plug different paging roots or completion paths.

Memory-management state centers on a current root plus history and per-mode bases. It holds a pointer to the active walk descriptor, a root descriptor with a mirrored host address and role, a small array of previous roots, and separate top-level pointers for legacy extended, four-level and five-level formats. A format record defines which bits must read as zero in shadow entries, covering both hardware-reserved positions and positions the shadow implementation never uses.

Each performance counter is described by kind, index, pause and interrupt flags, several count fields and linkage to host resources. One field holds a base value relative to consumed host counts rather than the live guest-visible value, so reprogramming can be deferred across guest writes. A second field accumulates emulation-triggered events awaiting overflow handling. Selector shadows, a current configuration used only for host event creation or reuse, and pointers to the host event and owning virtual CPU complete the record.

Counter taxonomy and capacity are fixed facts. The general type has value zero and the fixed type is the next enumerant. General capacity is eight on Intel and six on AMD with the effective maximum being the larger of the two. Fixed capacity is three on Intel and zero on AMD with the effective maximum again the larger. A generic maximum helper yields the greater of its two operands for these derivations.

Virtualized performance monitoring aggregates versioning, control shadows, per-counter records and several index bitmaps. It tracks architectural general and fixed counts, available event types, fixed-control and global control or status values with reserved-bit shadows, a two-word counter mask and a raw event mask. General and fixed counter arrays are sized by the effective maxima. Bitmaps record reprogramming requests, valid indices, in-use indices, instruction or branch counting, and mode-specific enable support. Debug-store, precise-event and cross-mapping state plus deferred-cleanup and programmed-event accounting complete the unit.

Several update rules keep host and guest counter views consistent. The reprogram-request bitmap shares storage with a wide atomic so all bits can be set in one access when filters change. A guest counter remapped to a differently indexed host counter loses precise-event capability while remapped. That remap mask must be refreshed after interrupts are disabled and before host guest-event collection. Host events not marked in use are released at most once per virtual CPU slice under a cleanup gate, and a programmed-event tally lets idle guests skip that scan.

Three debug-register mode bits are defined as low powers of two. The first marks breakpoints enabled, the second marks exits suppressed for debug registers, and the third marks hardware-automatic save and restore across guest transitions with host values reloaded on exit and architectural init values visible during exit handling.

Memory-type state mirrors variable and fixed range registers plus a default type. The variable portion holds paired base-mask entries, while fixed coverage is split into one large granularity block, two medium blocks and eight small blocks. A separate hypervisor identification record captures only a base leaf and a limit, defining the window a guest may query for hypervisor discovery.

Xen emulation per virtual CPU combines hypercall and run-state tracking with cached shared pages and timer support. It records a hypercall instruction pointer, current run state, upcall vector, last steal time, entry time and four accumulated run-state durations, plus pending-selector bits and identifiers. Four shared-page caches cover virtual CPU info, time info and two run-state areas. Timer state includes virtual interrupt, expiry in guest epoch, a pending count, a high-resolution timer, a poll channel and a poll timer, alongside a hypervisor identification window.

A deferred exception is a compact record separating control flags from payload. It indicates whether delivery is pending, whether injection was already attempted, and whether an error code or an extra payload word is present, then carries the vector number, the error code and the payload value. Later virtual CPU state holds two such records, one for guest injection and one for synthesized exits to the outer guest.

Kernel-only capability leaves form an ordered extension after the architecture capability words. The sequence starts at the architectural word count and proceeds through a fixed list of extended leaves before defining a total count and a derived kernel-only word count as the difference between that total and the architectural base. Implementations size the per-virtual-CPU capability array by the total.

Per-virtual-CPU architectural state starts with general registers, instruction pointer and availability or dirtiness bitmaps, then control registers with guest-owned and reserved-bit masks, protection keys, flags, extended feature enable, debug control and local APIC linkage. Interrupt handling adds a kernel chip pointer, a pending end-of-interrupt map flag, a handled-vector bitmap, attention bits, arbitration priority and multiprocessor state. Machine-check, microcode, capability, single-step and retry-address fields plus miscellaneous control registers round out synchronous execution context.

Practical execution support groups paging, floating point, emulation and identification. Paging keeps a current pointer plus distinct roots for non-nested and nested translation, two walk contexts for nested-physical and guest-virtual conversion, legacy pointer storage and five allocation caches including one for externally allocated tables. Floating point keeps guest state with host key bits handled separately alongside extended control and supported masks. Emulation keeps a context pointer, register-sync flags and userspace-completion context. Identification keeps entry count, entry array, dirty tracking, compatibility flag and the effective capability array.

Timekeeping separates guest, host and virtual views with explicit offsets and scaling. It stores a guest time value, paravirtual clock multiplier and shift with host frequency and shared-page cache, steal-time nesting, and layered translation offsets for outer and current guests with last-seen stamps, adjustment, generation counters and catch-up flags. Virtualized frequency uses its own shift, multiplier and rate, while adjustment, power-control and scaling-ratio shadows allow migration-safe updates.

Guest visibility and nested entry obey conservative guards. The capability array denotes effective permission, normally requiring both kernel and userspace consent, except for virtualization holes the kernel cannot block where the feature reads as present regardless, while features needing no kernel mediation pass through verbatim from userspace tables. A pending nested-enter marker must not be interrupted by a synthesized exit before the inner guest is entered, since exits only occur at instruction boundaries apart from a special notification exit that can disturb state. The marker uses distinct trusted and untrusted encodings to detect impossible userspace-stuffed exits. Direct userspace loading of legacy pointers is separately flagged.

Slot-level paging metadata tracks reverse mappings and large-page eligibility per page size. One reverse-map head array covers every supported size, a large-page info array covers all but the smallest size with a per-entry disallow flag, and a write-tracking array records guest frame protection. This lets the memory manager locate mappings, decide when a huge page must be split, and notice writes for dirty tracking.

Reference-time page setup moves through five observable phases. It begins unset when never configured or disabled, advances to guest-changed after the guest writes the control register or to host-changed after host-side initiation, reaches set once the page is active, and falls to broken if the configured guest address cannot be accessed. Transitions into changed states signal that a refresh is owed before the page can be trusted.

Host Hyper-V state serializes guest-visible enlightenments and crash reporting. It holds a lock, guest identity, hypercall and reference-time page addresses with the lifecycle status above, crash parameter block and control, a cached reference-time copy, a connection-to-event table, re-enlightenment and timestamp-counter emulation controls with status, an invariant-counter control, a mismatch count for virtual-processor numbering, an auto end-of-interrupt user count, a synchronous-debug unit whose inner block carries control, status, send, receive and pending page addresses plus an options word, and a one-time feature-check flag.

Host Xen state centers on versioning, shared info and event channels under a dedicated lock. It records version, long-mode and run-state-update flags with an upcall vector, a shared-info cache, an event-channel port table and a per-virtual-CPU poll mask sized by the maximum virtual CPU count, plus a hardware-virtual-machine configuration record. The lock orders updates to shared mappings and channel allocation against concurrent virtual CPU paths.

Mutual exclusion is partitioned by subsystem with documented nesting. Hyper-V and Xen host blocks each have a private mutex. The APIC map has its own mutex while virtualization updates use a read-write semaphore separating rare inhibit toggles from frequent checks. Shadow unsynchronized-page marking has a dedicated spinlock that is always taken even when the outer memory lock is already held for write, for uniformity. Timestamp writes use a raw spinlock because one protected counter is read with preemption disabled. Reference-time reads use a sequence counter. Time-division root list and link updates use a separate spinlock that remains useful inside the outer lock for code simplicity.

Virtual-machine-wide x86 state starts with memory-manager sizing, validity generation, type and protection flags, a page hash, an active-page list and per-flavor lists of zapping candidates with counts. Noncoherent DMA accounting, bypass-interrupt estimation, legacy chip pointers, non-maskable-mode accounting, APIC map with dirty tracking, access-slot toggles and virtualization inhibit reasons follow, with the most write-heavy virtualization counters isolated on their own cache lines away from read-mostly controls.

Remaining virtual-machine state covers clocks, quirks and optional accelerators. It holds wall clock, disabled-exit mask, clock offset, last and current timestamp snapshots with generation and matched-CPU tally, default rate and user-override flag, bus cadence, master-clock snapshot with rate limiter, Hyper-V or Xen sub-blocks when enabled, backward-clock and boot-clock flags, bootstrap identifier, quirk mask, chip mode with reserved-pin count, local-APIC presence and extended-APIC toggles, broadcast controls, mapped-input-output and platform-info flags, payload and fault-event toggles, bus-lock and monitoring switches, notification window, emulation-error policy, userspace register mask with filter, hypercall-exit mask, provisioning flag, event filter, huge-page recovery thread with cursor and once guard, and on 64-bit a time-division root list with leak accounting under proving builds.

Mode selectors use small dense enumerations. Interrupt-chip presence distinguishes none, in-kernel when that build option exists, and split configurations. Broadcast suppression distinguishes legacy-quirked, enabled and disabled behaviors. Memory-manager flavor distinguishes shadow and, on 64-bit, time-division tables before a count terminator. Pending nested entry uses one for trusted and two for untrusted. The reference-time lifecycle uses zero for unset with four further ordered phases.

Several comments warn against assuming success or stability. Clearing a candidate huge-page list does not guarantee a huge page will form, since later guest execution or backing-store shape can forbid it. Time-division roots stay linked until their reference count reaches zero and are freed only after a grace period, so readers must use read-copy-update or the memory lock correctly. Bits that cannot be virtualized remain visible despite configuration. Cross-mapped counters silently lose precise-event support. Notification exits can corrupt state if they interrupt pending nested entry. Userspace-provided register state can encode impossible exits that must be detected rather than trusted.

The fragments publish architectural contracts for other subsystems rather than code entry. They define the walk and memory-manager descriptor shapes with their callback signatures, the monitoring aggregate and its sizing maxima, the per-virtual-CPU and per-virtual-machine state shapes for x86 including Xen and Hyper-V extensions, the interrupt-chip and memory-manager selectors, the noncoherent-DMA presence marker, and the reference-time lifecycle enumeration. Consumers program against these layouts and enumerations while owning dossiers provide behavior.
